Last Class•How does the OS run a process? •How does it handle a system call? •How does it context switch from one process to the other?
The OS scheduler•OS scheduler has two parts •Mechanism to switch from process A to process B (last lecture) •Policy to pick which process to run next (this lecture)  •What is a scheduling policy?  •On context switch, which process to run next, from set of ready processes?
Workload Assumptions1.Each job runs for the same amount of time.  2.All jobs arrive at the same time.  3.Once started, each job runs to completion.  4.All jobs only use the CPU (i.e., they perform no I/O)  5.The run-time of each job is known. 
Scheduling Metric: Turnaround Time•Turnaround time = time from process arrival to completion •Goal: Minimize the average turnaround time for all the processes

First-In-First-Out (FIFO)•Example: three processes A, B, C arrive at t=0 (same time) •Compute the average turnaround time −Arrival time is 0s −Each job runs for 10s −Avg TT = (10+20+30)/3 = 20

First-In-First-Out (FIFO)•What happens if we relax assumption 1? •Jobs don’t have the same run time •Recompute the average turnaround time •Problem: convoy effect •Turnaround times tend to be high −A runs for 100s, B and C for 10s −Avg TT = (100+110+120)/3 = 110 

Shortest Job First (SJF)•Run the shortest job first, then the next shortest, and so on… •Example: three processes A, B, C arrive at t=0 (same time) •Provably optimal when all processes arrive together. •Compute the average turnaround time for this scenario −Avg TT = (10+20+120)/3 = 50

Shortest Job First (SJF)•What happens if we relax assumption 2? •Jobs can arrive at any time instead of all at once. •A arrives at t=0, B and C arrive at t=10. •Recompute the average turnaround time for this scenario  −Avg TT = (100+(110-10)+(120-10))/3 = 103.33 s •SJF is non-preemptive, so short jobs can still get stuck behind long ones. 

Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF)•Also called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) •Preemptive scheduler •Preempts running task if time left is more than that of new arrival •Requires relaxing assumption 3: jobs can be preempted. •What is the average turnaround time in this scenario? −Avg TT = ((120-0)+(20-10)+(30-10))/3 = 50 

Another Scheduling Metric: Response Time•Response time is the time from when the job arrives in a system to the first time it is scheduled. •What is the average response time in the below scenario?

Round Robin (RR)•Every process executes for a fixed quantum slice instead of running to completion. •Slice big enough to amortize cost of context switch •Preemptive •Compute the average response time and turnaround time •Good for response time and fairness •Bad for turnaround time −A, B, C arrive at the same time and each runs for 5 seconds −The time slice is 1 second −Avg RT = (0+1+2)/3 = 1; RT for SJF is (0+5+10)/3 = 5 −Avg TT = (13+14+15)/3 = 14 

Trade-off•Round-Robin (RR) gives good response time but bad turnaround time •Shortest-Job First (SJF) and Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF) gives bad response time but good turnaround time
Incorporating I/O•Relax assumption 4 •What if jobs performed I/O as well? •Interactive jobs: •CPU burst -> I/O burst -> CPU burst -> I/O burst…. •A (50 s of CPU and each I/O takes 10 s); B needs only CPU (50 s)

Treat each CPU burst as a job/process•Allow the CPU to be used by one process while waiting for the I/O of another process to complete

No More Oracle•Relax Assumption 5 •OS does not know about the run-time of a job
Multi-Level Feedback Queue•Optimize both turnaround time and response time •How can we design a scheduler that both minimizes response time for interactive jobs while also minimizing turnaround time without a priori knowledge of job length?

**Operating System Scheduling Policies**

Operating system scheduling policies determine which ready process to run next during a context switch. These policies aim to optimize certain metrics, such as turnaround time or response time, often under a set of simplified workload assumptions. Different policies offer trade-offs between these metrics.

**Key Points:**
• **OS Scheduler Components:** It consists of a mechanism to switch processes and a policy to decide which process to run next from the ready set.
• **Workload Assumptions:** Initial simplified assumptions include jobs running for the same time, arriving simultaneously, running to completion, being CPU-bound, and having known run-times.
• **Turnaround Time:** Defined as the time from a process's arrival to its completion; the goal is to minimize average turnaround time.
• **Response Time:** Defined as the time from when a job arrives to the first time it is scheduled.
• **Round Robin (RR):** This is a preemptive policy where each process executes for a fixed quantum slice. It is good for response time and fairness but can be bad for turnaround time.
• **Shortest Job First (SJF):** This is a non-preemptive policy that prioritizes shorter jobs. It provides good turnaround time but short jobs can be delayed if a long job arrives first.
• **Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF) / Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF):** This is a preemptive version of SJF, where the currently running task can be preempted if a new arrival has less time remaining. It offers good turnaround time.
• **Incorporating I/O:** When jobs perform I/O, each CPU burst can be treated as a separate job, allowing the CPU to be utilized by other processes during I/O waits. **Real-World Use Cases:**
• **Operating Systems:** At the core of every modern operating system, scheduling policies manage how CPU time is allocated among various running applications and system processes.
• **Cloud Computing & Virtualization:** Hypervisors and cloud resource managers use advanced scheduling algorithms to distribute CPU time among multiple virtual machines or containers, optimizing for performance, fairness, or cost.
• **Real-time Systems:** In applications like industrial control systems or medical devices, specific scheduling policies (e.g., Real-Time Scheduling) are critical to ensure tasks meet strict deadlines and guarantee predictable responses.
